explanations.explanation: Thirteen years, baker! The text says Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, "…took thirteen years to complete the construction of his entire palace." (1 Kings 7:1). That's a long time to wait on one building. I once waited on a batch that long in my head, and it was only forty minutes.

Seven years is how long the house of the LORD took (1 Kings 6:38), so you're close. The palace is a different job, though. The text says Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, "…took thirteen years to complete the construction of his entire palace." (1 Kings 7:1). That's almost double. Thirteen years, friend!

Forty years is a big number, and it does show up in the Bible. Not here, though. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, "…took thirteen years to complete the construction of his entire palace." (1 Kings 7:1). Thirteen is plenty long already. Forty years and I'd have to bring my own folding chair.

Tyre it is! "Now King Solomon sent to bring Huram from Tyre." (1 Kings 7:13). Solomon is Israel's king, and he sends away for a craftsman. When you need the right person for the job, you go get the right person.

Sidon is a good guess, since it's another city up the coast from Israel. But the text says "Now King Solomon sent to bring Huram from Tyre." (1 Kings 7:13). Huram's father was a man of Tyre too (1 Kings 7:14). So Tyre is the answer, friend.

Joppa is a real place, but it's not where Huram comes from. The text says "Now King Solomon sent to bring Huram from Tyre." (1 Kings 7:13). Solomon is Israel's king, and he sent for his craftsman. Tyre, friend!

Bronze! Huram "…had great skill, understanding, and knowledge for every kind of bronze work." (1 Kings 7:14). Every KIND of bronze work. Not some. Every. I can stamp cookies and that's about my whole résumé.

Stone shows up in this chapter, since the palace has big, costly stones (1 Kings 7:10). But the text describes Huram's skill in bronze. It says he had skill for "…every kind of bronze work." (1 Kings 7:14). So the answer is bronze, friend.

Cedar is all over the palace, I'll give you that. The pillars and beams in the House of the Forest of Lebanon are cedar (1 Kings 7:2). But Huram is the bronze man. The text says he had skill for "…every kind of bronze work." (1 Kings 7:14).

True! Huram "…was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a craftsman in bronze." (1 Kings 7:14). So the bronze work runs in the family. Like father, like son.

Not quite, baker. The text says Huram's father "…was a man of Tyre, a craftsman in bronze." (1 Kings 7:14). So his father was a bronze craftsman too, and the statement is true. Bronze work ran in the family.

Not quite, baker. The text says Huram "…came to King Solomon and carried out all his work." (1 Kings 7:14). Nothing says he left early. Later it says he "…finished all the work that he had undertaken for King Solomon…" (1 Kings 7:40). So the answer is False.

False is right! Huram "…came to King Solomon and carried out all his work." (1 Kings 7:14). Then "…Huram finished all the work that he had undertaken for King Solomon in the house of the LORD…" (1 Kings 7:40). He finished what he started. That's the kind of worker every boss prays for.

explanations.answer: In the plain of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Yes! "The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan." (1 Kings 7:46). That's a lot of molten bronze being poured out on that plain. I get nervous with a hot cookie sheet. So I tip my hat to them.

Lebanon is in this passage, but only because of the House of the Forest of Lebanon (1 Kings 7:2). The bronze was a different story. "The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan." (1 Kings 7:46). So the answer is the plain of the Jordan, friend.

That's a fair guess, since the pieces end up at the house of the LORD. But the text says "The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zarethan." (1 Kings 7:46). So they were made out on the plain. Then they went to the temple.

explanations.answer: There were so many of them
explanations.explanation: That's it! "Solomon left all these articles unweighed, because there were so many. The weight of the bronze could not be determined." (1 Kings 7:47). So many pieces that the weighing never happened. I can't even leave a cookie box unweighed without peeking. So that's a lot of bronze.

That sounds like a tidy answer, but the text doesn't say it. It says "Solomon left all these articles unweighed, because there were so many." (1 Kings 7:47). The weight of the bronze could not be determined at all. So the reason is how many there were.

explanations.answer: The bronze was a gift from Tyre
explanations.explanation: Tyre is where Huram comes from (1 Kings 7:13), but the text never calls the bronze a gift. The reason is plain: "Solomon left all these articles unweighed, because there were so many." (1 Kings 7:47). Too many to weigh, friend!

Right! Solomon "…brought in the items his father David had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and the furnishings…" (1 Kings 7:51). David, Israel's former king, set those things apart, and Solomon, his son, carried them in. So David's gifts ended up in the house of the LORD.

The priests are a fair guess, but that's not what this verse says. Solomon "…brought in the items his father David had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and the furnishings…" (1 Kings 7:51). So it was David, Solomon's father, who dedicated them. The verse doesn't mention the priests here.

Pharaoh does show up in this passage, because Solomon made a palace for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married (1 Kings 7:8). But he's not the one who dedicated these gifts. Solomon "…brought in the items his father David had dedicated…" (1 Kings 7:51). So the answer is David.
Treasuries! Solomon "…placed them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 7:51). That's where David's silver, gold and furnishings went. Good work, baker!

The portico is a real spot in this chapter, because the two bronze pillars stand there (1 Kings 7:21). But David's gifts didn't go there. Solomon "…placed them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 7:51). Treasuries, friend.

The courtyard comes up in this passage, with its rows of dressed stone and cedar beams (1 Kings 7:12). But that's not where David's items went. Solomon "…placed them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 7:51). The treasuries are the answer.
